title: TA8-18163
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons I reject the refugee claim of, XXXXXXXXXXX, a 37 year old citizen of Romania. Allegations:

The claimant alleges that after returning from Italy, he was beaten at a market. The claimant reported the beating to the police. After not receiving any response from the police, he returned to the police station where, he, as a Roma, was treated with distain. When the claimant complained he was taken to a back room and beaten and then thrown out of the station.
The claimant received medical attention and at some point, made a complaint of his treatment at the hands of the police to the Military court.

A few weeks later, the same police officer caught the claimant as part of a round up and threatened the claimant that he and his family, would be set on fire because of the complaint the claimant filed.

In XXXXXX 2007, the claimant's house was set on fire. In XXXXXX 2008, the claimant came to Canada and filed a refugee claim fearful of further actions by the police and others that would cumulatively constitute persecution. Determination
Did the claimant return to the police station to inquire as to the status of the investigation into his report of the beating? I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, he did not.

In his Personal Information Form (Exhibit C-1) narrative, the claimant recounts one time after 2 months that he returned to the police station. In oral evidence, he initially recounted he returned after 2 weeks. When asked to explain the inconsistency he testified he returned on 3 occasions, after 2 weeks, after 2 months and after 3 months. Initially, he was clear that after 2 weeks when he returned to the police station, he was beaten only once during the 2 week visit. After recounting the 3 visits, the claimant was asked which visit resulted in the beating, he recounted it was after the 2 month visit. The claimant's explanation as to why there is only a mention of one visit in his PIF narrative was he did not know he was to write everything. That is partially true. However, the instructions of question 31 of the PIF are clear that all attempts to seek state protection are to be included. If the claimant returned 3 times to the police then I would expect this to be clear in his PIF. Further if the claimant was beaten for 6 hours with a bat as he outlines in his PIF narrative, it is not plausible that he would return a month later for possibility more of the same.

I am satisfied due to the omissions from the PIF narrative and the inconsistency as to the number of police visits that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant did not inquire as to the status of the investigation into his original report.

Was the claimant beaten by the police? I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, he was not. The claimant's PIF narrative indicates he was beaten with a bat for 6 hours. In oral evidence he recalls being beaten by a phone book. He explained he was beaten by both a bat and a phone book. I don't accept that if he was beaten with a bat that he would recall the phone book first. The injuries by a bat and the pain would be much more severe. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied the claimant is creating the story of the police beating him to advance a refugee claim.

Was the claimant's house set on fire by the police or others following the directions of the police? I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, this is not the case. In oral evidence the claimant testified he saw the two men who threw an incendiary device at his home to set the fire. He testified he would recognize them if he saw them again, but he never saw them before or after they set the fire. In his written evidence, the claimant states he was walking home when he saw his house was on fire. The claimant's explanation for the omission/inconsistency was he was stressed from travel and may not have written everything down. If the house was set on fire by persons the claimant saw then he would not have written, when he was returning home he saw his house on fire and make no mention as to how the fire started. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that if the claimant's house was burnt, that the claimant did not know the cause and he created the story of the incendiary device to advance his refugee claim.

The claimant, when recounting the events after visiting the doctor, after being beaten by the police, omitted telling the medical authorities he had made a complaint against a police officer to the Military court. He first stated that after 2 or 3 weeks his house was set on fire then told of being threatened by the same police officer if he did not withdraw his complaint. The claimant's explanation for omitting mention of making a complaint at the Military court was that it was not a Military court. His explanation as to what the sentence in his PIF narrative meant when he stated, I proceeded for the Military Court afterwards and filed a complaint against the police officer, was that he went to the city to file a complaint. If that were the case, then I would have expected him to tell that after he left the doctor's office he made a complaint about the conduct of the police officer. Since the claimant failed to mention in his oral evidence that he made a complaint, I am satisfied it is more probable than not, that he did not.
Due to the numerous problems with the claimants evidence, I am satisfied he was not a credible witness.

In Exhibit C-2, there are a number of claims specific documents. The first is a report from Internal Affairs in Bucharest, indicating a complaint was registered. In the claimant's account, there is no mention he made a complaint in Bucharest. The document is a form letter where blanks have been completed. There is no indication as to the nature of the complaint. Hence, I give this document insufficient weight to offset my credibility concerns.

The second document states the exact causes of fire are unknown and the claimant reported the fire was caused by neighbours. Since this is inconsistent internally and with his other evidence, I give this insufficient weight to advance the claim on its own.

The final document is an electronic version of a news report. The original of the report may have some probative weight however an electronic version is too easily altered or created to be given weight. Further, much of the article relies on the statements of the claimant who I have found not to be credible.

Finally, counsel submitted that country conditions could support a Roma claimant even if the claimant was found not to be credible. I do not agree. In a country such as Romania, a member of the European Union, it is necessary for all claimants to establish state protection to be inadequate. Although there are references in Exhibit R/A-1, item 2.1 to when the state efforts have failed individual Romas in the past there is no independent credible evidence that for this claimant, if he required the assistance of the authorities in the future, that such assistance would not be forth coming.
For all the above, I find that the claimant has failed to establish there is a serious possibility he would be persecuted or suffer other forms of serious harm should he return to Romania today.

The Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
